[H1]So what's it about?[/H1]
In POE you are a criminal sentenced to death but instead shipped to the cursed continent of Wraeclast. You start with nothing and end up fighting Gods and other divine being. But to get there you will go through many beautifully crafted levels with many systems. At first it is intimidating and for your first run I highly recommend using a guide from for example [url=https://mobalytics.gg/poe/builds] Mobalytics [/url].

POE is an older game but can be measured against new releases as it has received and continues to receive updated. I've been an avid fan of Diablo and Diablo 2 since they were released (I was one of the first in D2 in Europe to hit lvl 99 back in the day). D3 was OK but not what I was looking into an ARPG and I've avoided D4 ever since the "don't you have phones" and all of the monetization; it's clear the Blizzard of old is no longer there.

POE is F2P but it doesn't mean P2W. Every couple of months new supporter packs are released that are time limited. But they are just cosmetics and the game comes with plenty. Only buy those if you want to support the developers. At most you probably spend about £30 to make your life easier with more inventory tabs but only gets those after you've played the game for a while and it's still not required for the first play through but it will help a lot managing all the loot you collect later on. Consider the campaign the trial or demo version to see if the game is for you.

You pick one of the available 7 classes when you start the game. As you progress you can then further specialise the class in the direction you like. There is so much to choose from that it will keep you busy for a long time. 

The campaign has 10 acts and those are really just the tutorial to avoid overloading you with the many systems POE has. After that the real game begins and it's all about completing maps at an increased difficulty for better rewards. Following that you arrive at the real end-game. It's a big game for sure :-).

It's great solo but multiplayer is good too. There is even PVP if you're interested in that. 

[H1]The good[/H1]
It has the most extensive systems I have ever seen in any ARPG. Just the skill tree alone is massive. This allows for a lot of experimentation to find the ideal setup. Your class is just a starting point and you can adjust how you feel fit.

I love the voice acting, the enemies and the graphical effects; GGG voice actors and artists are some of the best in class. 

There are many different leagues you can play (comparable to seasons in other games), including hard core and you can build even your own if you feel like.

The developers play their game and there are frequent updates. Tournaments are organised and if you watch them on Twitch you even get nice stuff from time to time.

The inner loot goblin is always satisfied when doing one of the many side activities in game. There is so much to collect and there is a variation of activities to keep it all fresh. 

You have your own hideout that you can decorate as you please. Later this becomes your central hub.

There is in-game trading with other players and multiplayer is supported. There is also a [url= https://www.pathofexile.com/trade ]trade post [/url] where you can buy and sell items you want or find.
The game plays really fast at times - much higher speed than D2; which is great it’s a constant adrenaline rush. The drawback is if your build has a weakness there is little room for error on the high end levels as it leaves you with little time to counter act.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
There is definitely a deep learning curve hence I advise using a guide for the first play through so you get an understanding of the basics. 

End game (lvl 90 - 100) can be really challenging depending on your build. Some require expensive (as in rare items they are player trade) to be effective and the AI will relentlessly punish you if you have a weak build to the point you want to give up. 

To counter this you probably want to start with a character that is less depended on gear and more on skills which are easier to come by. A second build could be one that is more depending on gear as you can use the first character to farm where necessary. In general: ranged class / skills are easier than melee especially later in the game.

For every new character you create you need to go through all 10 acts of the campaign; thankfully because of the stash, your hideout and all the other different game modes, including the progress in the second part (Atlas) is account wide it's not a major issue but it would be better if you would be given the option to skip the whole campaign after the first time that you've completed it (similar to like GW2 for example).

I disapprove of the lootbox mechanic introduced every season. It's not required, it's not in your face but it can cause serious issues for people that are vulnerable to gambling addiction. The positive maybe is that all the loot from the loot boxes are released later in the MTX store but still it should not be in the game.

[H1]The DLCs[/H1]
There are no DLCs other than supporter packs that only add cosmetics to the game. There is a microtransactions (MTX) store to buy cosmetics and QoL items. If you want to get any of those wishlist them and wait for a sale (every couple of weeks). Note that some of the MTX from POE is compatible with POE2 in particular most of the inventory tabs. 

[H1]Summary[/H1]
The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second best time is now. This is true for POE. I wish I had discovered it earlier but I'm happy I did eventually. If you're into ARPG it's one of the best games to get. Highly recommended.

Title: A Masterclass in Isometric Malice, Grinding Incompetence, and Betrayed Devotion: The Absolute Extinction Event of Path of Exile

I used to believe in this game with every fiber of my being. That unwavering, misplaced faith is now my deepest, most agonizing, and most humiliating wound. I didn’t just play Path of Exile; I consumed it, breathed it, and sacrificed thousands of waking and sleeping hours to its dark, fog-choked atlas corridors, treating its punishing skill trees and brutal map grinds as a sacred second home. I spent years defending Grinding Gear Games' glacial patch cycles, actively rationalizing their glaring resistance penalties, and aggressively dismissing the dark warning signs whispering through the community as the mere whining of disgruntled casuals. I was a foot soldier of a cult-like devotion, utterly convinced that this was a world crafted by visionary indie creators who understood the fragile, beautiful bond between an ARPG developer and a passionate player base.

How intensely, unforgivably, and pathetically foolish I was.

What the public sees on the store page is a legendary, deep-as-an-ocean action RPG—a modest isometric masterpiece born from years of dedicated work claiming to channel the ultimate hardcore ARPG experience. But beneath that paper-thin, calculatedly deceptive facade lies a predatory, aggressively hostile ecosystem designed to exploit your time, weaponize your passion, harvest your free community wiki labor, and ultimately punish you for the singular crime of actually engaging deeply with their high-tier endgame loop. The harsh reality of Path of Exile isn't a love letter to the genre; it’s an institutionalized insult, a middle finger to anyone foolish enough to invest hundreds of hours into its structurally hollow and fundamentally broken framework.

Let’s pull back the curtain and talk about the unspoken horror that haunts the upper echelons of this game: the arbitrary, indiscriminate, and utterly cowardly ban hammer and trade restrictions that target the most dedicated players the moment they master currency farming or fast mapping. For weeks, the veteran group chats whispered about it in paralyzing dread. Dedicated players—the exact backbone of the economy, the people organizing multi-stash trading syndicates, keeping multiplayer trade websites alive, and filling the community forums with complex build guides—would vanish overnight, or find their accounts locked behind an impenetrable wall of developer silence. Their names were silently scrubbed from ladders, their stash tabs vaporized, and their accounts flagged for abnormal macro usage. I scoffed at the victims. I arrogantly told myself that I played completely legitimately, that hundreds of hours of honest boss killing, meticulous currency management, and raw survival persistence would serve as my shield.

Then my inevitable turn came.

At level 98, deep inside a high-tier heavily-modded map I had rolled a thousand times for an elusive, mathematically insulting rare drop, the screen seized violently. The dreaded, ominous network disconnection warning flashed across the UI, followed instantly by a forced, unceremonious dump to the login screen. My hands shook uncontrollably as I scrambled to re-enter my credentials, hit enter, and was greeted by the most infuriating, gut-wrenching, soul-crushing message any ARPG veteran can possibly receive: “This account has been banned.”

No warning. No specific rule violation cited. No log data provided. No human review whatsoever. Just an abrupt, summary execution carried out by a completely inept, automated detection algorithm that apparently cannot comprehend the basic reality that a human being might actually want to play an ARPG for more than ten hours a day or use third-party trade macros. If you dare to actually play their game, to push past the lazy mid-game wall, and dedicate real, unbroken hours to mastering the convoluted passive skill tree and grinding endgame bosses, their broken, hair-trigger security protocols automatically flag your sheer dedication as anomalous botting behavior. They don't want you reaching the summit because they either haven't built a functional, stable endgame to sustain high-level players, or they are utterly terrified of what veteran players discover when the illusion of depth is finally pulled back.

And when you turn to customer support for even a shred of recourse or human dignity? Prepare to crash headfirst into a brick wall constructed entirely of corporate apathy, cowardice, and condescension. I poured my bleeding, broken heart into a meticulously written support ticket—detailing my exact playtime, my absolute adherence to fair play, and my profound, heartbreaking disappointment. Within minutes, I was hit with the exact same robotic, copy-pasted wall of garbage text that every single banned victim receives: "Your account has been reviewed and the suspension is permanent. This decision is final."

No appeal process. No human being willing to look at your case, check your server logs, or grant you basic respect. Just a cold, algorithmic middle finger from developers who happily take the community promotion, the active player counts, and the free labor of their trade systems while treating us like disposable trash the moment an automated script misfires. The silence from Grinding Gear Games is deafening, pathetic, and entirely telling. They hide behind automated systems because facing the human wreckage of their broken anti-cheat and abysmal balance design requires a spine they simply do not possess.

The technical and design state of the game outside of these tyrannical bans is an absolute disaster anyway, propped up by pure sunk-cost fallacy and endless supporter pack monetization. The economy is a chaotic, hyper-inflated mess dictated by market manipulators who somehow bypass the very detection tools meant for honest players. High-level combat balancing is practically non-existent, featuring lazy one-shot mechanics that demand artificial difficulty rather than tactical engagement. The repetitive grind quickly morphs from an exciting loot hunt into an unrewarding, punishing, soul-crushing chore. Every single system feels half-baked, held together with digital duct tape and the nostalgic goodwill of players who desperately want it to succeed, only to be brutally kicked in the teeth the second they cross the finish line.

My level 98 character—complete with painstakingly optimized passive trees, hard-earned mirror-tier equipment, hundreds of hours of irreplaceable memories, and genuine friendships forged in guild chats—was erased in a single, callous click. All of it gone, vaporized into the ether by developers who couldn’t care less if every single veteran player walked away.

If you are a new player currently looking at this store page, reading the glowing expansion promises, or thinking about downloading this free-to-play trap: Stop. Do not install it. Do not give them your metrics. Do not invest your time, your energy, or your passion into a digital world that fundamentally despises its own community. Play literally anything else. Because if you actually stay, if you actually grind, and if you dare to love this game too much, the only reward waiting for you at the top is a permanent ban screen and a developer who refuses to look.

Path of Exile isn't just another failed live-service experiment; it is a meticulously constructed psychological trap for the devoted and an eternal monument to bad-faith development. Save your time, save your sanity, protect your peace, and stay far, far away from this toxic wasteland. It stands as a profound, unforgivable insult to anyone who ever believed that passion, time, and genuine emotional investment in a virtual world would be met with anything other than cold, mechanical betrayal. Every single pixel of this fraudulent project bleeds contempt for its player base, transforming what should have been a nostalgic sanctuary.

I played this game many years ago when there were only 3 Acts. Over a decade and 7 additional acts later, it is most impressive how much content has been added to the game at no cost. The campaign is a well written grim tale about choices and consequences rather than your standard good vs evil plotline. You can play all 10 Acts without having to spend a penny. You may not buy a single cosmetic, however, you may need to invest in extra storage to play endgame content given the copious amounts of loot and currency you will reap. Endgame activities include Atlas of Worlds, Mine Delving, Rogue Harbor Heists, and Sanctum runs to name a few. GGG even added a City Management sim with Kingsmarch. Seasons add new gameplay modes and mechanics to incentivize rolling a new Exile. The most recent season has added a game changing quality of life improvement - the removal of skill gem and gear socket color matching restrictions. An absolute game changer! PoE has now evolved into one of the best ARPGs out there. I am hooked and loving it!

[h1]GREAT GAME - BUT ONE LEAGUE WAS ENOUGH FOR ME[/h1]

I played one league from beginning to end and honestly...

[b]I had a lot of fun.[/b]

Path of Exile has an insane amount of depth.

* Tons of builds
* Huge skill tree
* Very satisfying character progression
* Lots of endgame content
* A ridiculous amount of things to learn and optimize
* You can easily spend hundreds of hours on one character

But that is also where my biggest problem starts.

[h2]THIS GAME WANTS A LOT OF YOUR TIME[/h2]

Progression can become extremely time consuming.

Getting your build exactly where you want it, farming currency, improving gear and pushing further into the endgame can consume an enormous amount of time.

During my league I enjoyed doing it.

But after finally reaching my goals, my reaction was basically:

[b]"That was fun... but I don't think I want to do all of that again."[/b]

And with a new league, a huge part of that progression starts all over again.

For some players, that is exactly why they love Path of Exile.

For me, one serious league was enough.

[h2]GOOD:[/h2]

* Incredible build variety
* Deep character progression
* Huge amount of content
* Very satisfying when your build finally works
* You can play for a very long time without running out of goals
* One of the deepest ARPGs available

[h2]BAD:[/h2]

* Extremely time consuming
* Can be overwhelming for new players
* A lot of systems to learn
* Repeating the progression every league is not for everyone
* It can easily start feeling like a second job if you take it too seriously

[h2]FINAL VERDICT[/h2]

[b]RECOMMENDED.[/b]

I had a good time with Path of Exile and definitely got more than enough entertainment out of it.

But personally?

[b]I finished one league properly, reached my goals and I think that was enough for me.[/b]

**Recommended — 576+ hours**

Path of Exile is a wonderful game about killing monsters, collecting loot, and slowly realizing you've accidentally enrolled in an unpaid university course.

I started playing thinking, "Oh cool, Diablo but free."

576 hours later I'm staring at six different resistance numbers, moving gems around like a crackhead doing electrical work, and getting genuinely excited because a chest has the correct combination of coloured holes in it.

10/10.

I mostly play Necromancer, because why fight my own battles when I can bring an entire unemployment line of skeletons, spectres, golems and other assorted dead people with me?

Sometimes my army deletes half the map.

Sometimes a boss looks vaguely in my direction and I immediately become a historical event.

That's Path of Exile.

The amount of content in this game is fucking absurd. Every time I think I understand it, another mechanic crawls out from underneath a rock carrying seventeen currencies and a crafting system that apparently requires a minor in economics.

And somehow I love it.

The developers and support staff deserve genuine credit too. My experiences with them have been great. I've had reward/drop issues sorted out by actual humans, and I've always gotten the impression that the people behind this ridiculous monster genuinely give a shit about it and its community.

Is it beginner friendly?

Absolutely fucking not.

The passive tree looks like someone dropped a plate of spaghetti onto a motherboard and called it character progression.

But once it gets its claws into you, there really isn't anything else quite like it.

It's complicated. It's occasionally infuriating. It will happily murder you because you forgot that 41% chaos resistance is apparently the defensive equivalent of wearing a promising hat.

Then you'll get one beautiful drop and forgive everything.

Free game, by the way.

I've paid considerably more money for games I've played considerably less.

See you in maps.
